text: McTaggart's argument for the unreality of time turns on which alleged defect of the A-series?
choices: The A-series presupposes absolute simultaneity, which special relativity refutes.
Every event must be past, present, and future (incompatible properties), and the natural repair of relativizing them to times reintroduces the A-series, launching a vicious regress.
The A-series cannot order events that are simultaneous with one another.
The B-series is incoherent because 'earlier than' is not a genuine relation.
explanation: McTaggart argues the A-series is essential to time yet self-contradictory: each event has all three mutually exclusive A-properties, and analyzing this away as 'past at one time, future at another' presupposes a further A-series, generating a vicious regress. Option 0 imports a different, relativity-based objection to the A-theory; McTaggart's argument (1908) is a purely logical one that predates and is independent of special relativity.
